decks.title: Nature, Scope and Modes of International Business
goals: Explain what international business is and why it takes place
Describe its scope and its benefits to nations and firms
Explain the modes of entry with their merits and limitations
Choose a suitable mode of entry for an imagined firm

slides.heading: Nature, Scope and Modes of International Business
slides.body_md: Part 1: why firms and nations do business across borders, and how a firm can enter a foreign market.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what international business is, why it happens, its benefits, the modes of entry and choosing a mode

slides.narration: Why do firms sell, make and invest beyond their own country? In this part we study what international business is, why it happens, its benefits to nations and firms, and the modes of entry into foreign markets.

slides.heading: What is international business?
slides.body_md: **International business** means business activities, such as trade, manufacturing and investment, carried on across the boundaries of countries.

rows: Business activities carried on across national boundaries: trade, manufacturing abroad and investment
Exchange of goods and services between countries; one part of international business
Buying and selling inside the boundaries of one country

visual.alt: Table of three terms: international business as business across national boundaries including trade, manufacturing abroad and investment; international trade as exchange of goods and services between countries and one part of it; and internal trade as buying and selling inside one country
visual.caption: Trade is only one part.

slides.narration: International business means business activities carried on across national boundaries. These include trade, manufacturing abroad and investment. International trade, the exchange of goods and services between countries, is only one part of it. Internal trade, by contrast, stays inside one country.

slides.heading: Why does international business take place?

rows: A country lacks what another has in plenty
Kolmark has iron ore but little farmland
Workers and factories differ in output and cost
A Tesoria worker grows more tea than a Kolmark worker
Each country concentrates on what it makes best and trades for the rest
Tesoria grows tea; Kolmark weaves cloth

visual.alt: Table of three reasons for international business: unequal natural resources, differences in labour productivity and cost, and specialisation, each with an imagined illustration from Tesoria and Kolmark
visual.caption: Three reasons.

slides.narration: Three ideas explain why. Natural resources are unequal, so one country lacks what another has. Labour productivity and costs of production differ. And because of these differences, specialisation pays: each country concentrates on what it makes best and buys the rest.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: gains from specialisation
slides.body_md: Two imagined countries, each with a hundred workers, trade tea and cloth. See how the totals change.
bullets: Step 1: Find the output when workers are split equally.
Step 2: Find the output when each country specialises.
Step 3: Compare the totals.

rows: Tea (Tesoria 30 kg, Kolmark 10 kg a worker)
Cloth (Tesoria 10 m, Kolmark 20 m a worker)

visual.alt: Worked example table: with a hundred workers each split equally, Tesoria and Kolmark together make two thousand kilograms of tea and one thousand five hundred metres of cloth; after Tesoria grows only tea and Kolmark weaves only cloth, tea is three thousand kilograms and cloth is two thousand metres
visual.caption: Both totals rise.

slides.narration: In Tesoria a worker grows thirty kilograms of tea or weaves ten metres of cloth. In Kolmark a worker grows ten kilograms or weaves twenty metres. Split equally, the two countries make two thousand kilograms of tea and one thousand five hundred metres of cloth. If Tesoria grows only tea and Kolmark weaves only cloth, tea rises to three thousand and cloth to two thousand.

slides.heading: Scope of international business

rows: Goods sold to or bought from other countries
Kanchan Textiles ships sarees to Valmora
Services such as software, transport or tourism sold across borders
Pixel Path writes software for a foreign client
Giving others abroad the right to use know-how or a brand for a fee
Orchid Beverages licenses a recipe; Brisk Bites franchises cafes
Putting capital into a business in another country
Vega Labs builds a plant in Ostria

visual.alt: Table of four forms in the scope of international business with an imagined example of each: merchandise exports and imports, service exports and imports, licensing and franchising, and foreign investment
visual.caption: Four forms.

slides.narration: The scope has four parts. Merchandise exports and imports are shipments of goods. Service exports and imports include software and transport. Licensing and franchising give others the right to use know how or a brand. Foreign investment means putting capital into a business in another country.

slides.heading: Quick check: which form?
slides.body_md: An imagined software firm writes a program for a foreign client and is paid in foreign currency. Name the form.
slides.narration: Think about whether the foreign client receives goods or a service.

slides.heading: Benefits to nations

rows: Exports bring in currency that pays for imports
Each country makes what it makes best
Larger markets create output and jobs
People get more choice at lower cost

visual.alt: Table of four benefits of international business to a nation: earning foreign exchange, more efficient use of resources, growth prospects and employment, and a higher standard of living

slides.narration: A nation earns foreign exchange, which pays for imports. Resources are used more efficiently, because each country makes what it makes best. Growth prospects and employment improve, and the standard of living of the people can rise through more choice at lower cost.

slides.heading: Benefits to firms

rows: Foreign markets may pay better prices
Surplus output finds a buyer abroad
A wider market lets the firm expand
A way out of intense domestic competition
Dealing with foreign customers broadens outlook

visual.alt: Table of five benefits to a firm: prospects of higher profits, better capacity utilisation, growth prospects, a way out of intense domestic competition and improved business vision

slides.narration: For a firm, international business offers prospects of higher profits, better use of capacity, and growth prospects. It is a way out of intense competition at home, and dealing with foreign customers gives the firm an improved business vision.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: use of capacity
slides.body_md: Kanchan Textiles, an imagined firm, gets a foreign order. Find its use of capacity before and after.
bullets: Step 1: Divide home sales by capacity.
Step 2: Add the export order.
Step 3: Divide the new total by capacity.

visual.alt: Worked example table: looms can make five thousand sarees a month; three thousand sold at home is sixty per cent of capacity; an export order of two thousand sarees brings the total to five thousand, which is one hundred per cent
visual.caption: Use of capacity rises from 60 to 100 per cent.

slides.narration: Kanchan Textiles can weave five thousand sarees a month but sells three thousand at home, so its looms run at sixty per cent. An export order for two thousand sarees brings the total to five thousand, so capacity use rises to one hundred per cent.

visual.caption: Each step up brings more control, and more investment and risk.

slides.narration: This ladder shows the modes of entry. Moving up from exporting and importing, through contract manufacturing, licensing and franchising, and joint ventures, to a wholly owned subsidiary, the investment, the risk and the control all rise.

slides.heading: Exporting and importing

rows: The firm finds foreign buyers and ships the goods itself
Merit: keeps the whole sale. Limitation: needs export knowledge
An export house or agent in the home country finds buyers and ships
Merit: little effort or risk. Limitation: less control and a commission to pay
Buying goods from a supplier in another country
Merit: goods or inputs not made at home. Limitation: duties and delays

visual.alt: Table of exporting and importing as modes of entry: direct exporting where the firm ships itself, indirect exporting through an export house or agent, and importing, with a merit and a limitation of each
visual.caption: Low investment and low risk.

slides.narration: Exporting means selling goods abroad and importing means buying goods from abroad. In direct exporting the firm finds the buyers and ships the goods itself. In indirect exporting an export house or agent does this work. The merits are little investment and low risk. The limitations are transport costs, trade barriers and less control.

slides.heading: Quick check: indirect or direct?
slides.body_md: An imagined spice firm hands its cardamom to an export house that finds the buyers abroad. Name the mode.
slides.narration: Think about who finds the foreign buyers.

slides.heading: Contract manufacturing
slides.body_md: **Contract manufacturing:** a firm has goods made abroad by another firm to its specification, and sells them itself.

rows: A firm has goods made abroad by another firm to its specification and sells them itself
Low investment, quick entry, lower cost of making
Quality control is hard; trade secrets may leak
Lumen Apparel has Sutra Garments make its shirts

visual.alt: Table of contract manufacturing: a firm has goods made abroad to its specification and sells them itself, with merits of low investment, quick entry and lower cost, limitations of weak quality control and leakage of trade secrets, and the imagined example of Lumen Apparel and Sutra Garments
visual.caption: Another firm makes, you sell.

slides.narration: In contract manufacturing a firm has another firm abroad make goods to its specification, and then sells them under its own name. The merits are low investment and quick entry. The limitations are the difficulty of controlling quality and the risk that trade secrets leak.

slides.heading: Licensing and franchising

rows: Right to use a patent, trademark or know-how, for a fee
Right to run a business under a brand and system, for a fee
Little capital, quick entry, royalty income
Little capital, fast spread of the brand
The licensee may become a competitor
Poor service by one outlet can harm the brand
Brisk Bites and a local cafe owner

visual.alt: Table comparing licensing and franchising on meaning, merits, limitations and an imagined example: Orchid Beverages and Sagar Drinks for licensing, Brisk Bites and a local cafe owner for franchising
visual.caption: Rights granted for a fee.

slides.narration: In licensing, a firm grants a foreign party the right to use its patent, trademark or know how for a fee. In franchising, a foreign party runs a business under the brand and system of the franchiser. Both need little capital. The risks are loss of control, and a licensee who may become a competitor.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: income from licensing and franchising
slides.body_md: Find the royalty of an imagined licensor and the first-year income of an imagined franchiser.
bullets: Step 1: Take the royalty percentage of sales.
Step 2: Take the franchise share of monthly sales.
Step 3: Add the fee and twelve months of share.

rows: Orchid Beverages: 5 per cent royalty on sales of Rs 2,00,00,000
Brisk Bites: 4 per cent of monthly sales of Rs 6,00,000
Brisk Bites: fee plus twelve months of share

visual.alt: Worked example table: a five per cent royalty on sales of two crore rupees gives ten lakh rupees; a franchiser with an initial fee of three lakh rupees and four per cent of monthly sales of six lakh rupees earns twenty four thousand rupees a month and five lakh eighty eight thousand rupees in the first year
visual.caption: Royalty and fee income.

slides.narration: Orchid Beverages earns a royalty of five per cent on sales of two crore rupees, which is ten lakh rupees. Brisk Bites earns an initial fee of three lakh rupees and four per cent of monthly sales of six lakh rupees, which is twenty four thousand rupees every month. In the first year this is five lakh eighty eight thousand rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: the royalty
slides.body_md: An imagined licensor charges five per cent of sales of Rs 2,00,00,000. Find the royalty.
slides.narration: Work out five per cent of the sales.

slides.heading: Joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries

rows: A business set up and owned together by two or more firms
A foreign business in which the parent owns all the capital
Shared investment and risk; local knowledge
Partners may disagree; profits are shared
Heavy investment; the whole risk is borne by the parent

visual.alt: Table comparing joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries on meaning, merits, limitations and an imagined example: Dhanvantari Foods and Lindqvist Dairies, and Vega Labs in Ostria
visual.caption: Shared against sole ownership.

slides.narration: A joint venture is a business set up and owned together by two or more firms. It shares the investment and the risk, but partners may disagree. A wholly owned subsidiary is owned entirely by the parent. It gives full control but needs heavy investment and puts the whole risk on the parent.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: sharing a joint venture
slides.body_md: Two imagined firms build a joint plant. Find the capital and the profit of each.
bullets: Step 1: Split the cost in the agreed ratio.
Step 2: Split the profit in the same ratio.
Step 3: Check that the parts add up.

rows: Capital of Rs 50,00,000 in the ratio 60 to 40
Profit of Rs 8,00,000 in the same ratio

visual.alt: Worked example table: a joint plant costing fifty lakh rupees with capital in the ratio sixty to forty needs thirty lakh and twenty lakh rupees; a profit of eight lakh rupees is shared as four lakh eighty thousand and three lakh twenty thousand rupees
visual.caption: Profit follows the ratio.

slides.narration: A plant costing fifty lakh rupees is financed in the ratio sixty to forty, so the partners put in thirty lakh and twenty lakh rupees. A first year profit of eight lakh rupees is shared in the same ratio, giving four lakh eighty thousand and three lakh twenty thousand rupees.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the mode
slides.body_md: Match each imagined firm with the mode of entry that it uses.
slides.narration: Ask who makes the goods and who owns the business.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Trade, manufacturing and investment across borders; trade is a part
Unequal resources, differences in productivity and cost, specialisation
Merchandise, services, licensing and franchising, foreign investment
Foreign exchange, efficient resource use, growth, standard of living; profits, capacity, vision
Exporting and importing, contract manufacturing, licensing and franchising, joint ventures, wholly owned subsidiary

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: international business, reasons, scope, benefits and modes of entry

slides.narration: To sum up. International business is wider than trade. It arises from unequal resources, differences in productivity and cost, and specialisation. It benefits nations and firms. The modes of entry rise from exporting to a wholly owned subsidiary, with more investment, risk and control at each step.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give a merit and a limitation for every mode.
Use an imagined firm as the example.

rows: Treating international trade and international business as the same
Trade is one part of business across borders
Listing modes without a merit and a limitation
Give one of each for every mode
Licensing: right to use know-how; franchising: a whole business format
Using a real firm as the example

visual.alt: Exam tips table: four common mistakes about trade and business, merits and limitations, licensing and franchising, and real firm examples

slides.narration: Some tips. Do not treat international trade and international business as the same. For every mode of entry, give one merit and one limitation. Keep licensing and franchising apart. And use an imagined firm in your examples, never a real one.

sections.heading: 1. Nature of international business and why it takes place
sections.body_md:
**International business** means business activities, such as trade, manufacturing and investment, carried on across the boundaries of countries. **International trade**, the exchange of goods and services between countries, is one part of it.

**Why it takes place:**
1. **Unequal natural resources:** a country may lack what another has in plenty.
2. **Differences in labour productivity and cost of production.**
3. **Specialisation:** each country concentrates on what it makes best and buys the rest.

**Worked check:** with a hundred workers each, Tesoria and Kolmark together make 2,000 kg of tea and 1,500 m of cloth when workers are split equally, and 3,000 kg of tea and 2,000 m of cloth when each specialises.

sections.heading: 3. Modes of entry into international business
sections.body_md:
The modes rise in investment, risk and control:

1. **Exporting and importing**, direct or indirect. Merit: little investment and risk. Limitation: transport costs, trade barriers, less control.
2. **Contract manufacturing.** Merit: low investment, quick entry. Limitation: quality control, leakage of secrets.
3. **Licensing and franchising.** Merit: little capital, quick entry. Limitation: the licensee may become a competitor; loss of control.
4. **Joint ventures.** Merit: shared investment and risk, local knowledge. Limitation: disagreement between partners; shared profits.
5. **Wholly owned foreign subsidiaries.** Merit: full control. Limitation: heavy investment and the whole risk.

**Worked checks:** a 5 per cent royalty on Rs 2,00,00,000 is Rs 10,00,000; a joint plant of Rs 50,00,000 financed 60 to 40 needs Rs 30,00,000 and Rs 20,00,000.

sections.heading: 4. Export procedure
sections.body_md:
The standard sequence of an export:
1. Receipt of an enquiry and sending a quotation (proforma invoice).
2. Receipt of the order (indent).
3. Checking the importer's creditworthiness and securing a letter of credit.
4. Obtaining the Importer Exporter Code from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade and registering with an export promotion council (as of 2024).
5. Obtaining pre-shipment finance.
6. Production or procurement of the goods.
7. Pre-shipment inspection.
8. Obtaining a certificate of origin.
9. Reserving shipping space.
10. Packing and forwarding.
11. Insurance.
12. Customs clearance, through a shipping bill.
13. Obtaining the mate's receipt.
14. Paying freight and obtaining the bill of lading.
15. Preparing the invoice.
16. Securing payment, through documents sent via a bank against a bill of exchange.

**Dated note (as of 2024):** much of the paperwork is now filed electronically. A step of excise clearance in older books belongs to the older procedure and is not taught as current.

**Worked check (imagined):** 2,000 sarees at 25 US dollars is 50,000 US dollars; at an imagined Rs 80 to one US dollar it is Rs 40,00,000.

sections.heading: 5. Import procedure
sections.body_md:
The standard sequence of an import:
1. Trade enquiry.
2. Obtaining the Importer Exporter Code (as of 2024).
3. Arranging foreign exchange.
4. Placing the order (indent).
5. Obtaining a letter of credit.
6. Arranging finance.
7. Receipt of shipment advice.
8. Retirement of import documents.
9. Arrival of goods.
10. Customs clearance, through a bill of entry, and release of the goods.

**Worked check (imagined):** a machine of 12,000 US dollars plus 1,500 US dollars of freight and insurance is 13,500 US dollars, or Rs 11,07,000 at an imagined Rs 82; an imagined duty of 10 per cent is Rs 1,10,700, so the total cost is Rs 12,17,700.

sections.heading: 6. Export and import documents
sections.body_md:
1. **Commercial invoice:** the seller's bill.
2. **Packing list:** the contents of each package.
3. **Certificate of origin:** proof of the country where the goods were made.
4. **Shipping bill:** the exporter's declaration to customs.
5. **Mate's receipt:** the ship's receipt that the goods are loaded.
6. **Bill of lading or airway bill:** the carrier's receipt and evidence of the contract of carriage; a bill of lading is also a document of title.
7. **Marine insurance policy:** cover against loss in transit.
8. **Bill of exchange:** a written order to pay a sum.
9. **Letter of credit:** a bank's undertaking to pay against conforming documents.
10. **Bill of entry:** the importer's declaration to customs.

The documents and their forms are as of 2024.

key_terms.definition_md: A receipt issued by the ship's captain when goods are loaded.
A receipt and document of title issued by the shipping company after freight is paid.
A bank's undertaking to pay the exporter against documents that meet the terms.

sections.heading: 7. The World Trade Organization and other bodies
sections.body_md:
The **World Trade Organization** was established on 1 January 1995 and succeeded the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, which came into force in 1948. India is a founding member; the membership has grown to over 160 members as of 2024.

**Objectives:** raise standards of living and promote full employment; expand the production of and trade in goods and services; use resources sustainably; help developing countries to share in the growth of trade.

**Functions:** administer trade agreements; provide a forum for negotiations; settle disputes; review the trade policies of members; cooperate with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

**Benefits to members:** predictable rules; settlement of disputes; lower barriers; growth and incomes; fair treatment.

**Other bodies:** the **International Monetary Fund** (monetary cooperation, exchange stability, short-term help); the **World Bank** (loans for reconstruction and development); **UNCTAD** (helping developing countries to gain from trade and investment).

**Common mistakes**
- Treating international trade and international business as the same.
- Listing modes of entry without a merit and a limitation for each.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes international business?

options.text_md: Only the buying and selling of goods between two countries
All business activities, such as trade, investment and production, that are carried on across the boundaries of countries
Business that a firm carries on inside one state of its own country
A business that is owned by the government of one country

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** All business activities, such as trade, investment and production, that are carried on across the boundaries of countries. International business covers every business activity that crosses national boundaries, including making goods abroad and investing abroad, and not only trade. The second option is too narrow, the third describes domestic business, and the fourth is about ownership and not about crossing borders.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly relates international trade to international business?

options.text_md: International business is one part of international trade
The two terms mean exactly the same and nothing else is included
International trade means trade inside the boundaries of one country
International trade, the exchange of goods and services across borders, is one part of international business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** International trade, the exchange of goods and services across borders, is one part of international business. Trade across borders is one part of the wider activity called international business, which also includes investment and the licensing of know-how. The second option reverses the relation, the third wrongly equates the two, and the fourth describes internal trade.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined countries of Tesoria and Kolmark, a worker of Tesoria grows 30 kg of tea or weaves 10 metres of cloth in a season, while a worker of Kolmark grows 10 kg of tea or weaves 20 metres. Each country has 100 workers, split equally between the two goods. Now Tesoria puts all its workers on tea and Kolmark puts all its workers on cloth, and the two countries trade. Taken together, their output changes as follows:

options.text_md: Tea rises from 2,000 kg to 3,000 kg and cloth from 1,500 metres to 2,000 metres
Tea stays at 2,000 kg and cloth stays at 1,500 metres, because trade only moves goods
Tea rises to 3,000 kg but cloth falls to 1,000 metres
Tea falls to 1,500 kg and cloth rises to 2,000 metres

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Tea rises from 2,000 kg to 3,000 kg and cloth from 1,500 metres to 2,000 metres. Before, tea is 50 workers at 30 kg plus 50 at 10 kg, which is 2,000 kg, and cloth is 50 at 10 metres plus 50 at 20 metres, which is 1,500 metres. After specialising, Tesoria makes 3,000 kg of tea and Kolmark makes 2,000 metres of cloth, so both totals rise. The other options ignore the gain from specialisation or mis-state one of the totals.

questions.stem_md: Pixel Path, an imagined software firm of the imagined city of Chandrapur, writes an accounts program for a hospital group abroad and is paid in foreign currency. This activity falls under the scope of international business as
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a service export. Writing a program for a foreign client and being paid in foreign currency is the export of a service. Merchandise exports are goods that are shipped, nothing is invested abroad, and no brand or know-how is licensed.

questions.stem_md: Kanchan Textiles, an imagined firm of the imagined town of Sutrapur, can weave 5,000 sarees a month but sells only 3,000 at home, so its looms run at 60 per cent. A foreign order for 2,000 sarees raises the use of its capacity to 100 per cent. Which benefit to a firm does this show?

options.text_md: A way out of intense competition at home
A higher standard of living for the nation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Better utilisation of capacity. Looms that were partly idle now work to full capacity, which is better capacity utilisation. Escaping competition and a broader vision are other firm-level benefits that the case does not describe, and a standard of living is a benefit to a nation and not to one firm.

questions.stem_md: Meera Spices, an imagined firm of the imagined town of Elapur, hands its cardamom to Rasa Exports, an imagined export house, which finds the foreign buyers and ships the goods. Meera Spices has entered international business through
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** indirect exporting. Selling through an intermediary in the home country is indirect exporting. In direct exporting the firm itself finds the buyers and ships, no foreign firm makes the goods in contract manufacturing, and no overseas company is owned here.

questions.stem_md: Lumen Apparel, an imagined brand, designs shirts and has Sutra Garments, an imagined maker in the imagined country of Ostria, produce 10,000 shirts to its specification. Lumen Apparel then sells them under its own label. This mode of entry is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** contract manufacturing. Having a foreign firm make goods to your specification and selling them yourself is contract manufacturing. Licensing grants the right to use know-how for a fee, a joint venture is a business owned together, and an export house is an exporting intermediary.

questions.stem_md: Brisk Bites, an imagined cafe brand, lets a local owner in an imagined foreign city run a cafe under its name, menu and way of working, against an initial fee and a share of monthly sales. This is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** franchising. Letting another party run an outlet under a brand and system for a fee and a share of sales is franchising. Nobody manufactures to order here, the brand does not own the cafe, and no goods are exported.

questions.stem_md: Orchid Beverages, an imagined firm, licenses its recipe and brand to Sagar Drinks, an imagined firm abroad, for a royalty of 5 per cent of sales. If Sagar Drinks sells goods worth Rs 2,00,00,000 in a year, the royalty due is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Rs 10,00,000. 5 per cent of Rs 2,00,00,000 is Rs 10,00,000. The second value moves the decimal point, the third takes one fifth of sales, and the fourth is what remains after the royalty.

questions.stem_md: Dhanvantari Foods, an imagined Indian firm, and Lindqvist Dairies, an imagined firm abroad, build a joint plant that costs Rs 50,00,000, with capital in the ratio 60 to 40 and profit shared in the same ratio. If the plant earns a profit of Rs 8,00,000 in its first year, the share of Dhanvantari Foods is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Rs 4,80,000. 60 per cent of Rs 8,00,000 is Rs 4,80,000. The second value is the share of the foreign partner, the third splits the profit equally although the capital is not equal, and the fourth is the capital put in by Dhanvantari Foods.

questions.stem_md: Vega Labs, an imagined drug maker, puts all the capital into a plant in the imagined country of Ostria and owns every share of it. If the plant fails, Vega Labs alone bears the loss. Which limitation of a wholly owned foreign subsidiary does this show?

options.text_md: Having to share profits with a local partner
Heavy investment with the whole risk borne by the parent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Heavy investment with the whole risk borne by the parent. Owning everything means putting in all the capital and bearing all the risk. Sharing profit is a feature of a joint venture, loss of control is a worry with licensing and contract manufacturing, and an export house belongs to indirect exporting.

questions.stem_md: Two years after Orchid Beverages licensed its recipe to Sagar Drinks, an imagined firm abroad, Sagar Drinks begins to sell a similar drink under its own name. Which limitation of licensing does this show?

options.text_md: The licensor has to invest heavily in a plant abroad
The licensor has no income from the arrangement
The licensor has full control over the licensee
The licensee may learn the know-how and become a competitor

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The licensee may learn the know-how and become a competitor. A licensee that copies the know-how and sells on its own is the risk of creating a competitor. A licensor does not invest in a plant abroad, it earns a royalty, and it has limited control over the licensee, not full control.

questions.stem_md: Harbour Fabrics, an imagined importer in the imagined country of Valmora, asks Kanchan Textiles for the price of cotton sarees. Kanchan Textiles replies with a document that lists the goods, the price and the terms offered, and that does not ask for payment. The document is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** proforma invoice. A reply that sets out the goods, price and terms offered, without demanding payment, is a proforma invoice. A commercial invoice is the seller's bill that goes with the shipment, a bill of lading comes from the shipping company, and a certificate of origin names the country where goods were made.

questions.stem_md: Tarini Engineering, an imagined firm of the imagined town of Ranipur, sends a detailed order for a packaging machine, giving the make, the quantity, the price and the delivery terms. Such an order is called
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an indent. A detailed order for goods is an indent. A bill of entry is filed with customs, a mate's receipt is given by the ship's officer, and a proforma invoice is the seller's quotation and not the buyer's order.

questions.stem_md: Before Kanchan Textiles begins weaving, the bank of Harbour Fabrics undertakes in writing to pay Kanchan Textiles when the shipping documents match the agreed terms. This undertaking is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** letter of credit. A bank's written promise to pay the seller against conforming documents is a letter of credit. A bill of exchange is the seller's order to the buyer to pay, a shipping bill goes to customs, and a packing list describes the contents of packages.

questions.stem_md: On the strength of a confirmed export order of Rs 40,00,000, Kanchan Textiles borrows Rs 24,00,000 from its bank to buy yarn and pay weavers before the sarees are shipped. This step is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** obtaining pre-shipment finance. Funds borrowed to produce and pack goods before they are shipped are pre-shipment finance. Securing payment comes after shipment, retirement of import documents is an importer's step, and freight is paid to the carrier.

questions.stem_md: The customs of Valmora charge a lower duty on sarees made in India, and ask Kanchan Textiles for a paper proving where its sarees were made. The paper that Kanchan Textiles must obtain is a
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** certificate of origin. A paper that proves the country in which goods were made is a certificate of origin. A mate's receipt shows that goods were loaded, a bill of entry is filed by an importer, and a marine insurance policy covers loss in transit.

questions.stem_md: When the sarees of Kanchan Textiles are loaded on the ship, the captain hands the exporter a receipt that confirms the goods have come on board. This receipt is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the mate's receipt. The receipt that the ship's captain gives when goods are loaded is the mate's receipt. The bill of lading is issued by the shipping company after freight is paid, the shipping bill goes to customs, and the bill of exchange is an order to pay.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about a bill of lading is correct?

options.text_md: It is issued by the shipping company after freight is paid, and it serves as a receipt and as a document of title to the goods
It is issued by customs to allow an importer to clear the goods
It is the exporter's written order to the importer to pay a sum
It is a bank's promise to pay the exporter

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is issued by the shipping company after freight is paid, and it serves as a receipt and as a document of title to the goods. The shipping company issues it after freight is paid, and it acts as a receipt, as evidence of the contract of carriage and as a document of title. For goods sent by air a similar receipt is the airway bill. The other options describe a bill of entry, a bill of exchange and a letter of credit.

questions.stem_md: Kanchan Textiles files a document with customs to obtain permission to export its sarees, and Tarini Engineering files a document with customs to clear its imported machine. The two documents are, in that order,

options.text_md: a bill of entry and a shipping bill
a mate's receipt and a bill of lading
a shipping bill and a bill of entry
a packing list and a commercial invoice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a shipping bill and a bill of entry. An exporter files a shipping bill and an importer files a bill of entry. The second option reverses them, and the last two pairs are not filed with customs as the main declaration for clearance.

questions.stem_md: Tarini Engineering buys a machine for 12,000 US dollars from Berghof Machines, an imagined foreign maker, and pays 1,500 US dollars for freight and insurance. At an imagined rate of Rs 82 to one US dollar, it must also pay an imagined customs duty of 10 per cent on the total value in rupees. The total cost to Tarini Engineering is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Rs 12,17,700. The value in rupees is 13,500 times 82, which is Rs 11,07,000. Duty at 10 per cent is Rs 1,10,700, so the total is Rs 12,17,700. The second value leaves out the duty, the third takes duty on the machine alone, and the fourth is the duty only.

questions.stem_md: Harbour Fabrics, an imagined importer, orders 2,000 sarees from Kanchan Textiles at 25 US dollars each. At an imagined rate of Rs 80 to one US dollar, the value of the order in rupees is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Rs 40,00,000. The order is 2,000 times 25, which is 50,000 US dollars, and at Rs 80 each that is Rs 40,00,000. The second value is the amount in US dollars, the third forgets the price, and the fourth is the price of one saree.

questions.stem_md: Tarini Engineering pays the bill drawn on it and takes over the shipping documents from its bank so that it can claim the machine. Which step of the import procedure is this?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Retirement of import documents. Paying or accepting the bill and taking the documents from the bank is the retirement of import documents. Shipment advice is a notice from the exporter, foreign exchange is arranged before the order, and the order is placed before shipping.

questions.stem_md: The World Trade Organization was established on
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 1 January 1995. The World Trade Organization began on 1 January 1995. The date 1948 belongs to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, which the Organization succeeded, and the other dates are not linked to either.

questions.stem_md: The World Trade Organization succeeded an earlier arrangement that came into force in 1948. That arrangement was the

options.text_md: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
United Nations Conference on Trade and Development
International Bank for Reconstruction and Development

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade of 1948 was the forerunner of the World Trade Organization. The other three are separate bodies and were not replaced by it.

questions.stem_md: Brenmark, an imagined member country, says that a new tax on its tea by Altavia, another imagined member, breaks agreed trade rules. Talks fail, and Brenmark takes the matter to the World Trade Organization. Which function of the Organization is used?

options.text_md: Giving short-term loans to cover a payments gap
Fixing the exchange rate of a currency

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Settling trade disputes between members. Using agreed procedures to resolve a complaint between members is dispute settlement. Short-term loans are an International Monetary Fund function, project loans are a World Bank function, and the Organization does not fix exchange rates.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an objective of the World Trade Organization?

options.text_md: Fixing the prices at which members must sell their exports
Financing the building of roads and dams
Expanding the trade in goods and services
Setting the exchange rate for every currency

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Expanding the trade in goods and services. Expanding the trade in goods and services is one of its stated objectives. It does not fix export prices, project finance is the work of the World Bank, and exchange rates are not set by it.

questions.stem_md: The central bank of Ostria, an imagined country, faces a short-term gap in its payments to the rest of the world. It receives a loan from a body that also works to keep exchange arrangements stable among members. This body is

options.text_md: the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the International Monetary Fund. Short-term help for payment gaps and the promotion of exchange stability are the work of the International Monetary Fund. The World Bank lends for development projects, the conference body works on trade and development issues of developing countries, and the Trade Organization deals with trade rules.

questions.stem_md: Which body lends to member countries for reconstruction and development projects?

options.text_md: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
The World Bank (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The World Bank (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development). Lending for reconstruction and development projects is the work of the World Bank. The International Monetary Fund gives short-term help for payment gaps, the Trade Organization looks after trade rules, and the General Agreement was the older trade arrangement.

questions.stem_md: UNCTAD is the short form of

options.text_md: United Nations Council for Tariffs and Duties
Union of National Chambers for Trade and Development
United Nations Conference on Trade and Development
United Nations Committee on Trade and Defence

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** United Nations Conference on Trade and Development. UNCTAD stands for the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, which helps developing countries to gain from trade and investment. The other names do not belong to any such body.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.stem_md: When a firm has another firm abroad make goods to its specification and then sells them under its own name, the mode of entry is called ___ manufacturing.

questions.stem_md: When goods are loaded, the ship's captain issues the ___, and after freight is paid the shipping company issues the ___.

The seller's bill giving the goods, quantity and price

The details of what is inside each package

questions.stem_md: Match each international body with its main role.

Helping developing countries to gain from trade and investment

The goods are produced or procured

questions.stem_md: What is international business? Name any two forms in which it is carried on.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and two forms.

answer.model_answer_md: International business means business activities, such as manufacturing, trade and investment, that are carried on across the boundaries of countries. Two forms are merchandise exports and imports, and the licensing and franchising of know-how or brands.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish international trade from international business.
questions.solution_md: One line on trade and one on the wider scope of business.

answer.model_answer_md: International trade is the exchange of goods and services between countries, such as exports and imports. International business is wider: it includes trade and also manufacturing abroad, licensing and franchising, and investment in other countries.

marking_scheme.step: International trade is exchange across borders
International business is wider and includes investment and production

questions.stem_md: State two reasons why countries trade with one another.
questions.solution_md: Two reasons stated.

answer.model_answer_md: Countries differ in natural resources, so one may lack what another has in plenty. They also differ in labour productivity and cost of production, so each gains by specialising in what it makes best and buying the rest.

marking_scheme.step: Differences in productivity and cost, with specialisation

questions.stem_md: Explain any two benefits of international business to a nation.
questions.solution_md: Any two benefits explained.

answer.model_answer_md: A nation earns foreign exchange, which it can use to pay for imports. International business also allows a more efficient use of resources and creates growth and jobs, which can raise the standard of living of the people.

questions.stem_md: Lumen Apparel has Sutra Garments, a firm abroad, make its shirts to its own design. Name this mode of entry and state one limitation that Lumen Apparel faces.
questions.solution_md: Mode named and one limitation applied.

answer.model_answer_md: The mode is contract manufacturing. One limitation is that Lumen Apparel cannot supervise quality directly, so poor workmanship at Sutra Garments can harm its brand, and its designs may also be copied.

questions.stem_md: What is a joint venture? State one of its merits.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and one merit.

answer.model_answer_md: A joint venture is a business that two or more firms, often from different countries, set up together and own jointly. One merit is that the partners share the investment and the risk, and a local partner brings knowledge of the market.

questions.stem_md: What is a proforma invoice, and why does an exporter send it?
questions.solution_md: Meaning and purpose.

answer.model_answer_md: A proforma invoice is a document that lists the goods, price and terms an exporter offers, and it is not a demand for payment. The exporter sends it in reply to an enquiry, so that the importer can decide whether to place an order.

questions.stem_md: State any two functions of a bill of lading.
questions.solution_md: Any two functions stated.

answer.model_answer_md: A bill of lading is a receipt that the shipping company gives for the goods it has accepted. It is also evidence of the contract to carry them and a document of title, so the holder can claim the goods at the port of arrival.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a shipping bill from a bill of entry.
questions.solution_md: One line on each document.

answer.model_answer_md: A shipping bill is filed by an exporter with customs to obtain permission to export the goods. A bill of entry is filed by an importer with customs to obtain clearance of the imported goods and their release from the port.

marking_scheme.step: Shipping bill: exporter, permission to export
Bill of entry: importer, clearance and release

questions.stem_md: State any two functions of the World Trade Organization.
questions.solution_md: Any two functions stated.

answer.model_answer_md: The Organization administers the trade agreements among its members and acts as a forum for trade negotiations. It also settles disputes between members, reviews their trade policies and cooperates with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three forms in which international business is carried on.
questions.solution_md: Any three forms explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Merchandise exports and imports: the shipping of goods to and from other countries.
2. Service exports and imports: services such as software work or transport sold across borders.
3. Licensing and franchising: the grant of rights to use know-how or a brand abroad for a fee. Foreign investment is a fourth form.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three benefits of international business to firms.
questions.solution_md: Any three benefits explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Prospects of higher profits: foreign markets may pay better prices than the home market.
2. Better capacity utilisation: surplus output can be sold abroad, so plant does not lie idle.
3. A way out of intense competition at home, and improved business vision from learning about foreign markets.

questions.stem_md: Explain licensing and franchising as modes of entry, with two merits and one limitation of licensing.
questions.solution_md: Meaning of both modes, plus merits and a limitation of licensing.

answer.model_answer_md: In licensing, a firm grants a foreign party the right to use its patent, trademark or know-how for a fee. In franchising, a firm lets a foreign party run a business under its brand and system. Licensing needs little capital and gives quick entry, but the licensee may become a competitor.

questions.stem_md: Vega Labs, an imagined drug maker, plans to set up a wholly owned subsidiary in Ostria. State one merit and two limitations that it should weigh.
questions.solution_md: One merit and two limitations, each linked to the case.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Merit: Vega Labs keeps full control over operations, quality and its secret formulas.
2. Limitation: it must invest heavily in land, plant and staff, and bears all the loss if the plant fails.
3. Limitation: it is exposed to political and legal risks in Ostria, such as a change of policy.

questions.stem_md: Kanchan Textiles ships its sarees to Harbour Fabrics by sea. Name any three documents that it must prepare or obtain, and state the purpose of each.
questions.solution_md: Any three documents with purposes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Commercial invoice: the seller's bill that gives the goods, quantity and price.
2. Packing list: it shows what is inside each package, for customs and the importer.
3. Marine insurance policy: it covers the cargo against loss or damage at sea. A bill of lading or a certificate of origin would also do.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three benefits that a country gets by being a member of the World Trade Organization.
questions.solution_md: Any three benefits explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Common rules make trade more predictable, so exporters can plan.
2. A member can seek settlement of a dispute through agreed procedures, instead of being left to the strength of the other side.
3. Lower trade barriers bring a wider choice of goods and lower prices, and help trade and incomes to grow.

questions.stem_md: State the main role of the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and UNCTAD, one line each.
questions.solution_md: One role for each body.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The International Monetary Fund promotes monetary cooperation and stable exchange arrangements, and gives short-term help to members with payment gaps.
2. The World Bank lends to countries for reconstruction and development projects.
3. UNCTAD helps developing countries to gain from trade and investment.

questions.stem_md: Explain the benefits of international business to nations and to firms.
questions.solution_md: Three points for nations and two for firms, with explanation.

answer.model_answer_md:
To nations: 1. It earns foreign exchange, which pays for imports. 2. It allows more efficient use of resources, as each country makes what it makes best. 3. It brings growth and employment, and raises the standard of living.
To firms: 4. Prospects of higher profits and better use of capacity, since surplus output finds a foreign buyer. 5. Growth prospects, a way out of intense domestic competition and an improved business vision.

marking_scheme.step: Growth, employment and standard of living
Growth, escape from competition and vision

questions.stem_md: Explain contract manufacturing, joint ventures and wholly owned foreign subsidiaries as modes of entry into international business, stating a merit and a limitation of each.
questions.solution_md: Three modes explained, with merits and limitations.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Contract manufacturing: a firm has goods made abroad by another firm to its specification. Merit: low investment and quick entry. Limitation: quality control is hard and secrets may leak.
2. Joint venture: two firms set up a business together. Merit: shared investment and risk, and local knowledge. Limitation: partners may disagree.
3. Wholly owned subsidiary: the parent owns all the capital. Merit: full control. Limitation: heavy investment and high risk.

questions.stem_md: Describe the steps of the export procedure, from the receipt of an enquiry to the securing of payment.
questions.solution_md: Sixteen steps grouped into five stages.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Enquiry and quotation, receipt of the order, checking creditworthiness and securing a letter of credit.
2. Obtaining the Importer Exporter Code and registering with an export promotion council, then pre-shipment finance and production.
3. Pre-shipment inspection, certificate of origin, reserving shipping space, packing and insurance.
4. Customs clearance through a shipping bill, mate's receipt, freight and bill of lading.
5. Preparing the invoice and securing payment through a bank against a bill of exchange.

marking_scheme.step: Enquiry, order and letter of credit
Inspection, origin certificate, space, packing, insurance
Customs, mate's receipt, freight, bill of lading

questions.stem_md: Describe the steps of the import procedure, from the trade enquiry to the release of the goods.
questions.solution_md: Ten steps grouped into five stages.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Trade enquiry: the importer asks for quotations from suppliers abroad.
2. Obtaining the Importer Exporter Code and arranging foreign exchange through a bank.
3. Placing the order (indent) and obtaining a letter of credit.
4. Arranging finance, and receiving the shipment advice from the exporter.
5. Retiring the import documents, receiving the goods on arrival, and clearing customs through a bill of entry, after which the goods are released.

marking_scheme.step: Retirement of documents, arrival, customs clearance

questions.stem_md: Explain the purpose of any five documents used in an export or an import.
questions.solution_md: Any five documents with their purposes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Commercial invoice: the seller's bill giving goods, quantity and price.
2. Packing list: the contents of each package.
3. Certificate of origin: it shows where the goods were made, which may decide the duty abroad.
4. Bill of lading: receipt for the goods, evidence of the contract of carriage and document of title.
5. Marine insurance policy: cover against loss in transit. Others are the shipping bill, mate's receipt, bill of exchange, letter of credit and bill of entry.

questions.stem_md: Explain the objectives and the functions of the World Trade Organization.
questions.solution_md: Two points on objectives and three on functions.

answer.model_answer_md:
Objectives: 1. Raising living standards and promoting full employment. 2. Expanding the production of and trade in goods and services, using resources in a sustainable way, and helping developing countries to share in the growth of trade.
Functions: 3. Administering the trade agreements among members. 4. Providing a forum for negotiations and settling disputes. 5. Reviewing the trade policies of members and cooperating with the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

marking_scheme.step: Trade expansion, sustainable use, developing countries

questions.stem_md: Harbour Fabrics, an imagined importer, orders 2,000 sarees from Kanchan Textiles at 25 US dollars each. At an imagined rate of Rs 80 to one US dollar, find the order value in rupees, the pre-shipment finance of 60 per cent of that value, and the profit over a cost of Rs 1,400 a saree. Name the document by which Kanchan Textiles obtains customs clearance.
questions.solution_md: Order value, finance, profit and the document.

2. At Rs 80 to one US dollar, the order is worth Rs 40,00,000.

4. The cost is 2,000 times Rs 1,400, which is Rs 28,00,000, so the profit is Rs 12,00,000.
5. Customs clearance of the goods is obtained by filing a shipping bill.
